finding.claim: An unauthenticated client can force one blocking outbound HTTP fetch to the configured IdP token_keys endpoint per request by sending a Bearer JWT with a fresh random 'kid' header. The per-kid negative cache never hits for new kids, so the request thread blocks on the fetch before the signature is checked. This is resource exhaustion/amplification, not a signature bypass.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled 'kid' in the unverified JWT header of any request carrying an Authorization: Bearer header (src/Security/src/Authentication.JwtBearer/PostConfigureJwtBearerOptions.cs:63-65 passes keyId straight to ResolveSigningKey).
finding.sink: TokenKeyResolver.FetchKeySet -> httpClient.SendAsync to <Authority>/token_keys, executed synchronously via GetAwaiter().GetResult() (TokenKeyResolver.cs:106-113, 124).

trace.note: IssuerSigningKeyResolver lambda receives keyId from the token header before signature verification
GetTokenKeysUri builds <authority>/token_keys; the host is fixed by config, only the kid varies
cache lookup keyed by tokenKeysUri:kid; a new kid is a miss
cache miss triggers a synchronous FetchKeySet for every request with a new kid
negative result is cached only for that single kid (30-60s), so the next request with a different kid fetches again

finding.guards_checked: Issuer, audience and signature checks run after key resolution, so they do not stop the fetch. Authority host is config-pinned, so this is not SSRF. Negative caching is per kid, so it does not block fresh random kids. No concurrency lock or single-flight on FetchKeySet. No rate limiting found in the middleware path. Severity is low to medium: an unauthenticated request can hold a request thread for up to the backchannel timeout, and each request makes one outbound call to the IdP. Not verified at runtime; based on code reading of the Microsoft.IdentityModel resolver call order.
